## [Era one · 2010–2015 · R scripts]{.kicker} ElicitN

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
Software for structured expert elicitation.\
*Environmental Modelling & Software*, 2012.

::: {.minor .unread}
with R.A. O'Leary, S. Low-Choy, K. Mengersen & M.J. Caley
:::

::: {.arrows .say style="margin-top:0.5em;"}
- 25 R scripts of statistics
- 32 more running a Tcl/Tk interface
- distributed as a zip file, on SourceForge
- no package, no tests, no version control
:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}

::: {.say style="margin-bottom:0.3em;"}
Used it to estimate the number of species on coral reefs worldwide
:::

![](figures/reef-richness.png){.panel width="90%" fig-alt="Estimates of species richness on coral reefs worldwide with 95% credible intervals: 70,000 named species, 110,000 discovered but unnamed, 620,000 undiscovered, and 830,000 in total, with an interval from 550,000 to 1,330,000."}

:::

:::

::: {.punch .fragment style="font-size:1.1em; margin-top:0.4em;"}
Effectively unreproducible within [five years]{.e3}.
:::

::: {.minor .fragment style="text-align:center;"}
Five of us wrote the paper, three of them statisticians. None of us thought to ask whether it
would still run.
:::

::: {.notes}
Era one produced scripts, not software.

ElicitN was a real collaboration with three statisticians.

> Click: coral reef species.

Published in *Current Biology* in 2015.

> Click: unreproducible.

> Click: the last line.

[~45 s]
:::

## [Era two · 2015–2020 · Industry data and GitHub]{.kicker} Dredging thresholds

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}

::: {.say .unread}
Coral mortality at each site against water quality → a concentration–response curve from
field data
:::

::: {.say .fragment fragment-index="1"}
We used ROC curves to derive thresholds, as for any classifier: false alarms against missed
coral mortality
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index="2"}

::: {.say}
This allowed us to derive probabilistic thresholds linked to their purpose.
:::

::: {.say}
In this case we used probable mortality versus possible mortality thresholds to distinguish
management zones.
:::

:::

::: {.lede .fragment fragment-index="3"}
Still in regulatory use. The code was written for one project and never packaged.
:::

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

::: {.r-stack}
![](local/cr-curve.png){.panel .stack-panel fig-alt="Probability of coral mortality against light stress, a 14-day running mean, with a fitted S-shaped curve. Sites with low stress have near-zero mortality; sites with high stress have high mortality."}

![](local/roc.png){.panel .stack-panel .fragment data-fragment-index="1" fig-alt="An ROC curve of true positive rate, or statistical power, against false positive rate, or false alarm rate, with a high-power threshold and a low-alarm-rate threshold marked."}

![](local/management-zones.png){.panel .stack-panel .fragment data-fragment-index="2" fig-alt="The concentration–response curve with the probable and possible mortality thresholds marked as vertical lines, projected down onto a plot of impact against distance from the dredge, where they mark the edges of the zones of high impact, moderate impact and influence."}
:::

::: {.credit}
Fisher, Walshe, Bessell-Browne & Jones (2018) *J. Appl. Ecol.* 55:415. WA EPA (2016) Technical
Guidance: Environmental Impact Assessment of Marine Dredging Proposals.
:::

:::

:::

::: {.notes}
From those data we could fit concentration–response curves in the field rather than in a
laboratory.

> Click: ROC curves.

> Click: the impact zones.

> Click: the last line.

The code behind them cannot be separated from data I'm not able to share.

[~45 s]
:::

::: {.notes}
Era two was really two strands. On the left is the industry work: the data and the
regulatory stakes, with code that only works on data I can't distribute.

> Click: the packages column.

Alongside it I started putting packages on GitHub.

FSSgam began as a function for one paper and became a package because people kept asking
for it.

epower is a toolbox for the power of before–after control–impact designs, from an
industry-funded project with BMT.

Both are public and installable, and no regulation depends on either.

They could become packages because they were built on data I could share.

There were still no tests, and neither was on CRAN.

> Click: the last line and the separation graphic.

Separating a method from confidential data well enough to release it is a lot of work, and
this I think does remain a problem in open source software.

## [Era three · 2021 onwards · CRAN]{.kicker} Species sensitivity distributions

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="38%"}

::: {.say}
Default guideline values are the environmental equivalent of the
[0.05 blood alcohol driving limit]{.hl}.
:::

::: {.arrows .say}
- above the limit, activities must be stopped or modified
- below it, the environment is assumed to be "safe"
:::

:::

::: {.column width="62%"}
![](figures/ssd-model-average.png){.ssd-side fig-alt="A species sensitivity distribution fitted to CCME boron data on a log concentration axis, showing six thin candidate distribution curves, a bold model-average curve, and the PC95 guideline value marked at 1.26 mg/L."}
:::

:::

![](local/breath-test.jpg){.absolute .photo top="560" left="215" width="370" fig-alt="A police officer holding a breath-testing device to a driver."}

![](local/police-hat.png){.absolute top="705" left="128" width="150" fig-alt="A police cap."}

::: {.notes}
ssdtools is some of my more recent work that has had the biggest impact.

> Read the slide.

They are derived from a species sensitivity distribution, or SSD. Each point is the toxicity
estimate for one species, which is what bayesnec (my other software) was built to estimate.
You fit a distribution and read off the concentration that protects, here, 95% of species.

There is no theoretical basis for choosing one distribution, and ssdtools solves this by
averaging over several distributions.

[~60 s]
:::

---


## [Era three · 2021 onwards · CRAN]{.kicker} Evaluation of `ssdtools`

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="58%" .unread}

::: {.say}
Joint Australian–Canadian project, funded by the Australian Government (DCCEEW)
:::

::: {.arrows .say}
- David Fox, Environmetrics Australia
- Joe Thorley & Carl Schwarz, British Columbia
- `ssdtools` compared with **Burrlioz 2.0**
:::

::: {.minor}
Benchmark data sets, plus simulated data with a known true value, so that bias and
coverage could be measured.
:::

:::

::: {.column width="42%"}

::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index="2" .unread}

::: {.punch style="font-size:0.9em; margin-top:0.2em;"}
Recommendation:\
adopt `ssdtools` as the\
[default software]{.e3}
:::

::: {.minor style="text-align:center; margin-top:0.3em;"}
Australia · New Zealand · Canada
:::

![](local/anzg.png){.anzg fig-alt="Screenshot of the website of the Australian and New Zealand Guidelines for Fresh and Marine Water Quality."}

:::

![](local/shiny.png){.shiny .fragment data-fragment-index="2" fig-alt="Screenshot of the shinyssdtools web app fitting six distributions to a dataset, with the fitted curves plotted."}

:::

:::

:::

::: {.open-source .fragment fragment-index="1"}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="38%"}

::: {.punch style="font-size:0.85em; margin-top:0;"}
Essentially, three regulators\
cannot audit a [black box]{.e3}.
:::

![](local/black-box.png){.black-box fig-alt="A black box."}

:::

::: {.column width="62%"}

::: {.say}
Every expert could read the source code, run the benchmarks, and disagree about specific
lines.
:::

::: {.say .fragment fragment-index="2"}
Most people deriving guideline values don't write R. The Shiny app, `shinyssdtools`, is how
they use the method.
:::

:::

:::

:::

::: {.notes}
ssdtools was originally written by Joe Thorley and Carl Schwarz. The project's job was to
evaluate whether ssdtools could replace Burrlioz in the Australian guideline framework.

With a stated aim of collective agreement between the Australian and Canadian experts.

We compared the two on benchmark data sets, and on simulated data with a known true value, so
we could measure bias and coverage. ssdtools performed better, and including more
distributions improved its estimates. The recommendation to adopt it has since been
approved, and this is now in the Australian and New Zealand guidance.

> Click: open source.

This project is a good example of where open source software shines.

With a closed desktop program, the discussion ends up relying on trust in whoever wrote it.

> Read the slide.

> Click: the Shiny app.

[~90 s]
:::

## The change since June

::: {.lede style="margin-bottom:0.3em;"}
I stopped writing R code by hand in [June]{.e3}.
:::

![](figures/where-work-goes.png){.fig-full style="max-height:560px;" fig-alt="Stacked bar chart of files changed on a working day, by category, in three periods, measured from 2,374 authored commits across seven public repositories, on every branch except gh-pages. Before 20 June 2026, about 12 files a day over 302 working days; from 20 June to 28 July, about 29 a day over 11; from 29 July to 13 October, about 86 a day over 51. Beside each bar are its commits: 1,304, 78 and 992. As shares, tests rise from 3 to 17 and then 16 per cent, packaging and CI from 4 to 15 and back to 5 per cent, and source code falls from 41 to 23 and then 29 per cent."}

::: {.notes}
> Read the slide.

I now work with Claude Code or Codex, and my impression is that I'm about five times more
productive.

That is an impression, so I measured it.

On a day I worked on these packages, I used to change about 12 files. Since the end of July it
has been 86, mostly in bayesnec.

Tests went from 3% of those files to 16%.

So the change is not in the typing. The work around the code now gets done: the tests,
documentation and continuous integration that determine whether software still runs in five
years.

[~45 s]
:::

## `FSSgam`, 2018 to 2026

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="54%"}
First commit **14 September 2018**.

::: {.arrows}
- first test file: **20 June 2026**
- first CI workflow: **20 June 2026**
- **7 years and 9 months** with neither
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:0.6em; line-height:1.35;"}
Then, over **four days**: 32 commits, 9 test files, roxygen documentation, a pkgdown site,
`NEWS.md`, a snake_case interface with deprecation wrappers, and CRAN preparation.
:::

:::

::: {.column width="46%"}

::: {.punch .fragment style="font-size:1.1em;"}
Writing the tests found\
[two silent bugs]{.e3}\
present since 2018.
:::

::: {.lede .fragment style="text-align:center; margin-top:1.4em;"}
This package is now on CRAN.
:::

:::

:::

::: {.notes}
One package in detail. FSSgam's first commit was in September 2018, and it went seven years
and nine months without a test file or continuous integration. There was always a more
pressing deadline.

Both arrived on the 20th of June this year.

> Click: four days.

Over the next four days there were thirty-two commits, nine test files, documentation, a
pkgdown site and CRAN preparation.

> Click: two bugs.

Writing the tests found two bugs that had been there since 2018. A deprecated argument gave
the right warning and then did nothing. Two fields of the output came back NULL, because the
code read the wrong element names. Anyone using those features got the wrong result,
with no warning.

> Click: CRAN.

With a little extra work, most of it done by Claude,

> Read the slide.

> If running long, drop this slide and say the bugs paragraph over the previous one.

[~60 s]
:::

## Routine work and judgement

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Now routine

::: {.arrows}
- test suites
- vignettes that stay current
- refactoring code that works
- continuous integration
- responding to CRAN
:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}
### Still mine

::: {.arrows}
- is this the right model?
- is the answer plausible?
- what would show it is wrong?
- is it defensible to a regulator?
:::

:::

:::

::: {.lede .fragment style="margin-top:0.6em;"}
The standard used to evaluate `ssdtools` and Burrlioz applies to code written by a model:
read the source, simulate with a known answer, check bias and coverage.
:::

::: {.punch .fragment style="font-size:1.0em; margin-top:0.8em;"}
AI use in open source software is a rapidly evolving space.
:::

::: {.notes}
The left column is work that used to be put off for the next deadline, and now gets done.

> Click: still mine.

The right column has not changed. If anything it matters more, because I'm producing more
code for each hour of my own attention.

> Click: the standard.

When we evaluated ssdtools against Burrlioz, we asked for the source code, benchmarks, and
simulations with a known answer. I don't get to lower that standard because a model wrote the code. The
methods I used for checking someone else's software are the ones I now use for this.

> Click: a rapidly evolving space.

I think

> Read the slide.

It is for me.

[~50 s]
:::

## `bayesnec`, June to October 2026

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="42%"}

::: {.say .unread}
No commits from July 2025 until late June. Since then, 817.
:::

::: {.fragment}

::: {.say style="margin-bottom:0.1em;"}
Claude and Codex found 86 bugs and flaws: 47 in code people wrote before June, 27 in code
written since.
:::

::: {.minor style="margin-bottom:0.6em;"}
45 of the 47 are in the release on CRAN.
:::

:::

::: {.fragment}

::: {.say style="margin-bottom:0.1em;"}
Issues were opened about as fast as they were closed.
:::

::: {.minor style="margin-bottom:0.6em;"}
In June, 22 were open, some since 2020; all are now closed. Since then, 151 more were opened
from my account, by Claude, Codex or myself, and 135 of them closed.
:::

:::

::: {.say .fragment}
103 commits parked on a `predev` branch.
:::

::: {.lede .fragment style="font-weight:700; margin-top:0.5em;"}
Writing code is no longer the limit. Reading it is.
:::

:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
![](figures/bayesnec-weekly.png){.bayesnec-fig fig-alt="Two bar charts on the same weeks, June to October 2026. Commits a week in bayesnec: none in June, a few in July, rising through August to 173 and 211 a week in mid-September, then falling to 112, 24, one and none; most are merged into dev, and from the third week of September most are parked on predev. Issues a week: in each week from mid-August, about as many issues were opened as were closed, up to 29 opened and 37 closed in one week."}
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Things got very busy for the last month or so. I had to prepare a software training course I
was teaching at a conference, and decided to add some significant functionality to bayesnec
at the same time. Things rapidly escalated to the point where I was struggling to read and
check everything being done.

> Click: bugs in the original code.

Every feature or bug fix I tackled resulted in Claude finding more bugs and flaws, many of
them written by humans into the original software.

> Read the slide.

> Click: issues.

I ended up in an endless loop of trying to resolve issues, with Claude or Codex opening even
more issues as fast as they were closed.

> Click: predev.

I couldn't find the time to review everything before merging it to dev, so for now I resorted
to making a predev branch and parking it.

> Click: the limit.

I'm not exactly sure where things will go from here.

> Read the slide.

[~75 s]
:::

---


## Points to take away

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="57%"}

::: {.arrows style="font-size:1.0em; margin-top:0.5em;"}
- The maintenance that determines whether research software outlives its project now
  takes far less time.

::: {.fragment fragment-index="1"}
- We still have no good pattern for open, reusable tools built on
  [data that cannot be shared]{.e3}.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index="2"}
- AI now writes more than humans can feasibly review.\
  Understand what would show it is wrong, and build simulations and tests to check it.
:::

:::

:::

::: {.column width="43%"}
![](figures/known-answer-check.png){.check-fig .fragment data-fragment-index="2" fig-alt="Schematic of a cycle of four boxes. Known answer, set by you, drawn as a target. An arrow labelled simulate leads to simulated data, drawn as scattered points. An arrow labelled run leads to code written by AI, too much to read, drawn as many lines of code fading out. An arrow leads to estimates, one per data set, drawn as dots near the centre of the same target. A double-headed arrow between the estimates and the known answer is labelled compare: bias, coverage."}
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Three things I'd like to leave you with.

First, the tests, documentation and continuous integration that determine whether
research software outlives its project now take far less time. If you are using AI to work
faster, spend some of the time saved on this work.

> Click: data that cannot be shared.

Second, we still don't have a good pattern for building open, reusable tools on data that
can't be shared. That gap is where a large amount of high-quality industry data stops being
useful to anyone except the client. If you've worked on this problem, I'd like to talk to
you.

> Click: your review.

Third, AI is now producing more than we can realistically review. We need new ways of
thinking about what reviewing that should look like. For me, it is about understanding what
would show if it was wrong, and building simulations and tests to demonstrate that.

[~55 s]
:::
